cards.title: Start creative with a customer problem, not a format
cards.summary: Before choosing UGC, static or carousel, mine customer research to find one problem, then let the problem dictate the format.
cards.use_when: Kicking off a new paid-social creative round for a product and you don't yet know which angle or format to produce.
steps: Mine sources that already contain customer language: existing product reviews, comments under your own ads and social posts, support tickets, post-purchase survey responses, Reddit discussion, and competitor reviews and ad comments.

From those sources, extract three things: what the customer wants, what is stopping them from getting it, and what they have already tried (which reveals failed alternatives you can position against).

Example: for a compact walking pad sold to work-from-home buyers, reviews surface 'I sit at my desk 8 hours and barely move', 'I want a treadmill but don't have space', and 'I can't have something loud while I'm on calls'. Each is a ready-made ad angle.

Only after you have the problem do you choose a format. If the value is simple and instantly understood, a static image can carry it; if the value requires seeing it fold open, slide under a desk, or be used in real life, you need video.

Competitor reviews are especially valuable because they surface what rivals are failing at, giving you an objection to counter inside your ad and a differentiation angle beyond 'we have this and it's good'.
caveats: The source says it looks at these sources usually; treat it as a research menu, not a mandatory checklist.
Avoid starting the conversation from 'should we make UGC or a static' — the source calls that thinking backwards.

cards.title: Build one ad around one argument, not ten selling points
cards.summary: Packing every selling point into a single ad produces a confusing infomercial; instead pick the single argument for the persona and prove it.
cards.use_when: Writing the script or storyboard for a cold-traffic ad and the draft is accumulating warranty, returns, dimensions, motor speed and every other feature.
steps: Write the angle as a single sentence that states one argument for one persona, e.g. 'Get more steps while you work without a giant treadmill taking precious space.'

Make every element inside the ad support that sentence. If the ad is about space and portability, show the room still having space, show the pad sliding under the desk, show it folding or being moved to a closet.
Deliberately withhold logistics like the 30-day return, warranty and guarantee — the source notes the customer will learn all of that later on the landing page.

If the product is genuinely quiet enough for calls, a strong execution is a video of someone on an important call or interview, then the camera zooms out to reveal they are getting steps in — painting the value without talking about the treadmill itself.
Contrast this with a white-background product shot labelled 'at home treadmill': it shows the metal rectangle rather than the reason to buy.
caveats: A plain product rectangle image can still work for high-intent audiences who are already sold and are only deciding who to buy from and when; it is cold traffic that needs the picture painted.
One product can have ten reasons someone buys it and therefore ten angles — but that becomes ten separate creatives, budget permitting, not one giant ad.

cards.title: Match every product claim with visual proof
cards.summary: Any claim made in an ad script needs a corresponding on-screen demonstration, because audiences no longer trust bare assertions.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a finished creative before launch to check whether the claims in the voiceover or copy are actually demonstrated on screen.
steps: List every product claim in the ad, then for each one ask 'how can I prove this visually?'

If you say it's compact, show how small it actually is; if you say it fits under a desk, film it under a desk; if you say it stores easily, show someone putting it in an apartment closet or moving it, and consider showing an older (55+) user doing it to signal ease.
If a product claim is quantifiable and the brand has data to support it, show the actual number rather than the adjective.

Treat visual proof as the main selling mechanism: the source argues anyone can say 'this product changed my life' and that audiences, especially with widespread AI-generated copy, no longer trust it. The creative should do as much selling as possible visually.

This is also what separates an ad that gets clicks from one that gets buying behaviour: in the source's example, a 'routine / before-and-after / application' video explained what was being sold and produced website buying behaviour, while a visually stimulating but unexplained ad did not.
caveats: Only show a quantified number if the brand actually has the data to back it; otherwise it's an unsupported claim.
Do not confuse a visually proven ad with a highly engaging one — an ad that proves nothing can still rack up a very high CTR.

cards.title: Write hooks directly from the stated customer problem
cards.summary: Turn the researched customer complaint into the first line of the ad so the right viewer self-selects and keeps listening.
cards.use_when: Drafting hooks and opening seconds for a cold-traffic video ad after you have selected one customer problem.
steps: Convert the problem into a direct, qualifying hook, e.g. 'If you work from home and somehow finish the day with 800 steps when your goal was 10,000, keep listening.'
Follow with the solution in plain terms: the pad fits under a standing desk, lets you get steps in while working, and can be put away afterwards.

For video, show the whole process on screen: someone working at the desk, the pad underneath, them on a call, then putting it away. The source notes this sequence can carry the ad on its own without heavy text overlay.

Optimize for comprehension and self-recognition rather than cleverness: if the ad resonates with the viewer's life it clicks subconsciously, and hearing 'this solves my exact problem' is more powerful than making a cinematic ad that appeals to everyone.
Reuse the customer's own words from reviews and support tickets where possible, since those phrases are the ones that trigger recognition.
caveats: A direct problem-statement hook trades broad appeal for resonance; that is the intended trade-off for cold traffic, not a way to appeal to a general audience.
The source explicitly is not trying to be super clever — don't optimize hooks for wit at the expense of clarity.

cards.title: Generate more angles from consistently repeated review themes
cards.summary: Segmenting reviews by use case can multiply a single generic creative into several distinct, proven ad angles.
cards.use_when: A brand has one generic creative and wants more angles without inventing new positioning from scratch.
steps: Read reviews looking for clusters — the same use case or same job-to-be-done appearing repeatedly rather than one-off mentions.
In the source's blackout blinds example, reviews repeatedly showed nursery use, RV use, and truck drivers using them in their trucks.
Build separate creatives around each consistently mentioned use case rather than producing more variations of the generic blackout blind ad.
Prioritize which segments to produce first based on how often the theme appears and how well it lines up with the audience you can actually reach affordably.
caveats: The blinds example is illustrative of the method, not a guaranteed result; the value comes from the repeated pattern in your own reviews.
The source notes you need budget to afford building out multiple angles — it recommends building one angle to profitability first, then using side budget to test others.

cards.title: Match creative testing volume to your daily ad spend
cards.summary: Launching dozens of ads on a small budget means most never get distribution, so 'it didn't work' is not a real finding.
cards.use_when: Planning how many new creatives to launch this month given your current daily spend.
steps: Before producing or launching a batch, check daily spend. The source's rule of thumb: at 30, 50 or 100 dollars a day you cannot feed an unlimited number of ads enough spend to learn anything.

Launch a focused batch instead and give the platform enough opportunity to distribute spend and return a signal, so the next round of creative is based on real customer response rather than guesswork.

In the source's $30/day account example, 13 ads were launched and the impression limit was initially set to 1,000, then lowered to 800 because CPMs were averaging $50–70 and the test needed to finish efficiently without burning budget.
Aim to find winners within the first week to two weeks rather than waiting indefinitely for under-spent ads to prove themselves.
If most of a large batch never received spend, do not record them as failures — record the test as inconclusive and re-run fewer creatives with adequate distribution.
caveats: The 1,000 and 800 impression limits and the $50–70 CPM are the source's specific example from one newer account with a pixel that lacked data; your CPMs and therefore practical limits will differ.
The exact interface for setting impression limits and viewing distribution changes over time — verify the current ad platform controls.

cards.title: Don't crown the ad the platform spent the most on
cards.summary: An ad that receives the bulk of spend naturally drives the most sales, so 'winner' must be judged on supporting metrics, not volume.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a creative test where one ad has taken most of the spend and you are about to declare it the winner and scale it.
steps: Check whether the other ads genuinely received distribution. The source describes brands with small budgets launching 30 ads, declaring failure two days later, when in reality all spend kept going to the same single ad.

Recognize that the platform snowballs spend on an ad with a strong CTR, good link click-through rate and lower-than-average CPM, and will keep pushing it to $150, $200 or $400 — but that decision is the platform reacting to engagement, not proof of buying intent.
Instead of taking engagement at face value, watch the ad and understand why it is working, then check whether that reason relates to the product and its value.
Judge ads on the full supporting metric set, never on CPA or ROAS alone, so you can distinguish a genuinely scalable creative from one that merely had the most volume behind it.
Also ask whether the ad can hold spend at larger scale, because an ad that looks great at $30/day can fall apart as budget rises.
caveats: A good CPA does not automatically mean a good top-of-funnel ad — it may only work at low spend, or it may be better deployed as a retargeting creative.
The source states its opinion that CPA/ROAS alone is insufficient reasoning; treat this as its stated position rather than a universal platform rule.

cards.title: Read CTR and link CTR together to spot empty attention
cards.summary: A high CTR with a large CTR-to-link-CTR drop signals an ad that entertains but fails to explain the product.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing whether a high-CTR creative is actually driving qualified buying traffic or just capturing attention.
steps: Compare CTR against link click-through rate. The source's anchor example: an ad with a 10.9% CTR (described as very high for ecommerce) lost over 3% between CTR and link CTR, while a lower-CTR ad (6.3%) lost less than 2%.
Interpret a large CTR-to-link-CTR gap as people engaging with the video but not being primed enough to want to visit the site — the creative did not explain the product or its value.
Check post-click behaviour as well, including conversion rate, add-to-carts, checkouts, drop-off percentages and on-site behaviour, to confirm whether the traffic had buying intent.

Watch the ad itself to explain the numbers: the source's high-CTR example was visually stimulating (calming, cutting-style footage) but the viewer never learned what was being sold, while the lower-CTR ad showed the routine, the before-and-after, the application and what you actually buy.
Note that a viewer may not even be a potential customer for that product category — attention and purchase intent are different things.
caveats: Do not treat the 10.9% / 6.3% CTRs or the 3% vs 2% drop as benchmarks; they come from one account and one pair of ads.
Lower CTR with strong post-click behaviour can be the better ad; the conclusion is about the whole metric pattern, not CTR in isolation.

cards.title: Run single-variable creative tests within the same angle
cards.summary: Vary only the delivery format while holding angle and product constant so you can attribute the result to something specific.
cards.use_when: You have a promising angle and want to learn something rather than randomly produce new ads.
steps: Take one validated angle — e.g. 'get your steps in while you work without needing a giant treadmill' — and produce two versions that share the same product and argument.
Example pairing from the source: version one as a UGC video, version two as a carousel where the slides tell the story, with a different opening format but the same underlying angle.
Run them in an apples-to-apples environment where each gets equal visibility, then read the data to identify why one was better.
Never change the hook, angle, audience, landing page, offer, campaign and creative simultaneously — the source's point is that if performance changes you will have no idea which change caused it.

After isolating the winner, cut the weaker version and carry the learning into the next brief, focusing on how to make a better version of what worked (the source suggests more before-and-after and routine footage as a next step in its example).
caveats: The source acknowledges that video versus carousel is a large format difference; the principle is to control as much as possible, not that all format comparisons are perfectly clean.
Format is only a variable to test once the angle itself is defined — the source explicitly de-prioritizes starting from format.

cards.title: Diagnose creative through the attention-to-purchase journey
cards.summary: Trace each metric stage — stop, click, post-click behaviour — to locate where the ad or the site is actually failing.
cards.use_when: An ad is underperforming and you need to decide whether to rebuild the creative, the landing page or something else.
steps: First ask: did we get their attention? If nobody stops, the hook may be too weak or the visual itself is not interesting.

Second ask: did they click to the site? If people watch but nobody clicks, the creative may be entertaining but the product and its value are not compelling or not being communicated — possibly they don't understand why they need the product.

Third ask: what happened after the click? If an ad gets lots of quality clicks but nobody buys, do not blame the creative immediately — it may be a good ad acting as the vehicle to the website, with the problem sitting in landing page load speed or quality.
When investigating post-click problems, review conversion rate, add-to-carts, checkouts, offer, pricing, shipping and website experience.

Frame the whole system as a two-piece puzzle: the cost to acquire attention and the conversion rate. The source's illustration: sending a million people to a site converting at 0.5% can never be profitable because the cost of that traffic is too high.
caveats: The 0.5% figure is an illustrative example used to make the arithmetic point, not a benchmark or threshold.
Use the diagnostic order as a way to assign blame, not as a claim that only one stage can be at fault.

cards.title: Use each creative test as the brief for the next round
cards.summary: Every test result should specify what to produce next — more of a winning angle, more of a winning hook, or more of a winning format.
cards.use_when: Scheduling the next creative production round and deciding what the team should actually make.
steps: After each test, read the result as a production instruction rather than a score. If an angle worked, make more creatives around that angle; if one hook crushed the others, keep that hook and write three different video bodies after it.
If a format underperformed, follow the evidence — e.g. if review-style UGC lost but a simple product demonstration worked, explore more product demonstration creatives.

Feed competitor weaknesses into the brief: if competitor reviews show they handle something poorly, build an ad that counters that objection, giving you differentiation beyond 'we have this and it's really good'.

Use the source's closing formula for each round: choose one customer problem, write the angle in a single sentence, and make every line of the ad prove that sentence, then change one meaningful thing at a time.

Replace the vague weekly question 'can we get AI to make more static images?' — which the source says yielded no results over two weeks — with 'what did customers respond to last week and what should we make from it?'
caveats: This is the source's stated operating philosophy from managing paid ads across many brands, not a guarantee of results in any particular account.
The Monday cadence is the source's example of how to structure the review; the essential part is that the test output drives the next brief.

cards.title: Handpick ads into funnel positions based on supporting metrics
cards.summary: Individual winners serve different funnel roles, and the combination of metrics tells you whether an ad belongs at top, middle or bottom of funnel.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to deploy each winning creative — prospecting versus retargeting — and what budget structure to give it.
steps: Judge ads on the combined evidence of CTR, link click-through rate, CPA, post-click behaviour and whether the ad can hold spend at larger scale — no single metric assigns a funnel role.
Recognize that a strong CPA might simply mean an ad works at low spend, and that such an ad may be a strong retargeting candidate rather than a scalable prospecting ad.
Place each handpicked ad into the funnel position its metric pattern supports, then build the account structure around those placements so you get the result you want.
Continue watching whether promising ads hold up as budget increases, since an ad that performs at $30/day can fall apart on scale.
Where you don't yet have enough budget to place a full set into each position, prioritize the angle that pays for itself, then use side budget to test the remaining angles.
caveats: The source notes these decisions are made in its own service by refusing to take platform engagement at face value; the general principle is that funnel role is inferred from combined metrics, not from one number.
Metric thresholds vary by account; the source does not give universal funnel-placement cutoffs.

      "tags": ["paid-social-creative", "experiment-design", "creative-testing", "ugc", "carousel", "measurement", "creative-strategy"]
    },
    {
      "title": "Diagnose creative through the attention-to-purchase journey",
      "summary": "Trace each metric stage — stop, click, post-click behaviour — to locate where the ad or the site is actually failing.",
      "use_when": "An ad is underperforming and you need to decide whether to rebuild the creative, the landing page or something else.",
      "steps": [
        "First ask: did we get their attention? If nobody stops, the hook may be too weak or the visual itself is not interesting.",
        "Second ask: did they click to the site? If people watch but nobody clicks, the creative may be entertaining but the product and its value are not compelling or not being communicated — possibly they don't understand why they need the product.",
        "Third ask: what happened after the click? If an ad gets lots of quality clicks but nobody buys, do not blame the creative immediately — it may be a good ad acting as the vehicle to the website, with the problem sitting in landing page load speed or quality.",
        "When investigating post-click problems, review conversion rate, add-to-carts, checkouts, offer, pricing, shipping and website experience.",
        "Frame the whole system as a two-piece puzzle: the cost to acquire attention and the conversion rate. The source's illustration: sending a million people to a site converting at 0.5% can never be profitable because the cost of that traffic is too high."
      ],
      "caveats": [
        "The 0.5% figure is an illustrative example used to make the arithmetic point, not a benchmark or threshold.",
        "Use the diagnostic order as a way to assign blame, not as a claim that only one stage can be at fault."
      ],
      "tags": ["paid-social-creative", "measurement", "funnel-analysis", "conversion-optimization", "landing-page", "creative-testing", "checkout"]
    },
    {
      "title": "Use each creative test as the brief for the next round",
      "summary": "Every test result should specify what to produce next — more of a winning angle, more of a winning hook, or more of a winning format.",
      "use_when": "Scheduling the next creative production round and deciding what the team should actually make.",
      "steps": [
        "After each test, read the result as a production instruction rather than a score. If an angle worked, make more creatives around that angle; if one hook crushed the others, keep that hook and write three different video bodies after it.",
        "If a format underperformed, follow the evidence — e.g. if review-style UGC lost but a simple product demonstration worked, explore more product demonstration creatives.",
        "Feed competitor weaknesses into the brief: if competitor reviews show they handle something poorly, build an ad that counters that objection, giving you differentiation beyond 'we have this and it's really good'.",
        "Use the source's closing formula for each round: choose one customer problem, write the angle in a single sentence, and make every line of the ad prove that sentence, then change one meaningful thing at a time.",
        "Replace the vague weekly question 'can we get AI to make more static images?' — which the source says yielded no results over two weeks — with 'what did customers respond to last week and what should we make from it?'"
      ],
      "caveats": [
        "This is the source's stated operating philosophy from managing paid ads across many brands, not a guarantee of results in any particular account.",
        "The Monday cadence is the source's example of how to structure the review; the essential part is that the test output drives the next brief."
      ],
      "tags": ["paid-social-creative", "creative-strategy", "creative-testing", "experiment-design", "ad-angles", "hook-writing", "content-production"]
    },
    {
      "title": "Handpick ads into funnel positions based on supporting metrics",
      "summary": "Individual winners serve different funnel roles, and the combination of metrics tells you whether an ad belongs at top, middle or bottom of funnel.",
      "use_when": "Deciding where to deploy each winning creative — prospecting versus retargeting — and what budget structure to give it.",
      "steps": [
        "Judge ads on the combined evidence of CTR, link click-through rate, CPA, post-click behaviour and whether the ad can hold spend at larger scale — no single metric assigns a funnel role.",
        "Recognize that a strong CPA might simply mean an ad works at low spend, and that such an ad may be a strong retargeting candidate rather than a scalable prospecting ad.",
        "Place each handpicked ad into the funnel position its metric pattern supports, then build the account structure around those placements so you get the result you want.",
        "Continue watching whether promising ads hold up as budget increases, since an ad that performs at $30/day can fall apart on scale.",
        "Where you don't yet have enough budget to place a full set into each position, prioritize the angle that pays for itself, then use side budget to test the remaining angles."
      ],
      "caveats": [
        "The source notes these decisions are made in its own service by refusing to take platform engagement at face value; the general principle is that funnel role is inferred from combined metrics, not from one number.",
        "Metric thresholds vary by account; the source does not give universal funnel-placement cutoffs."
      ],
      "tags": ["paid-social-creative", "measurement", "funnel-analysis", "budget-allocation", "retargeting", "scaling", "ad-platform"]
    }

10-MCR / paid social creative and content

Goes here. Paid social creative production, hook writing, direct response video frameworks, creator/UGC scripting, static ad design, messaging strategies, evaluating stages of awareness, identifying new ad formats/angles, advertorials, unique mechanisms, and creative strategist workflows.

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details a systematic, research-backed creative testing process for e-commerce, emphasizing that ads must be built around a single customer problem with concrete visual proof rather than random volume generation. modules: [MCR] topics: [creative strategy, messaging and positioning, campaign setup and tracking] tier: 2 scope_hint: core

Topics. creative strategy / Building a structured creative process rooted in deep customer research (reviews, support tickets, competitor complaints) to identify what the customer wants, what's stopping them, and what they've already tried. Restricting each ad concept to communicate a single, focused argument or angle (e.g., getting steps in without needing a giant treadmill) rather than packing multiple selling points into an infomercial. Ensuring that every product claim made in the ad script is matched with concrete visual proof (e.g., showing the product sliding under a desk to prove it is compact). campaign setup and tracking / Establishing rigorous creative testing standards by matching creative testing volume to available ad spend. Avoiding false winners by analyzing supporting metrics beyond initial CTR—such as link click-through rate, drop-off percentages, and post-click website behavior—to verify whether an ad actually drives qualified buying intent or merely captures empty attention. Using single-variable testing (changing one meaningful element at a time, such as testing a UGC video against a carousel for the exact same angle) to isolate performance drivers and inform the next creative brief.

Look for. The primary danger of putting too many selling points into a single ad: it turns into a confusing infomercial instead of a focused argument. The definition of a "single-variable test" in creative testing: keeping the core angle and product identical while changing only the delivery format (e.g., UGC vs. carousel) to isolate what works. The core reason why a high CTR does not automatically mean a winning ad: visually stimulating ads can capture empty attention, but if they fail to explain the product value, the traffic will bounce without buying.

Skip. Promotional pitches to book a call with the speaker's agency (ADVT).

Scope mix. Almost all core.

Volume. 10 to 15.

A lot of e-commerce teams are making more ads than ever and still have no clear answer when someone asks, well, what should we make next? [music] One week they may copy a UGC ad they saw, the next week they try a static image, then [music] 15 more concepts go into the account, but the team can still not explain what the winners [music] proved outside of a couple just spending more. I've managed paid ads across more than 500 e-commerce brands in the useful creative process starts before anybody opens a camera or design file. We find one customer problem with evidence, build one clear angle around it, and test the creative in a way that gives you an answer. So, in this video, I'll build that process from thinking about your first creative to your next testing decision. So, each round teaches you what to make next and puts more budget behind ideas customers have actually responded to. Now, if we jump right into it, this may sound backwards, but when I'm thinking about creative, I'm not really starting with should we make UGC or should we have some sort of static ad or a carousel? And people say, well, those are types of creatives, right? Well, yes, but those are formats, how you deliver the message. I want to know, what are we trying to communicate in this ad? And so, before anybody opens Canva or starts filming, I want to understand the customer. Usually, I'm looking at things like existing reviews, customer comments on your ads or social media, support ticket you guys get, maybe sales calls if you're a SaaS or an info product, and some objections come up on the sales call itself. also look at post-purchase surveys you sent through email, Reddit can be a place you can find some customer discussion, competitor reviews, what are they not doing right, what are your customers for your competitors kind of complaining about, and even underneath those competitors' ads, what are some things that we can look at to basically identify three things. The first, what does the customer want? Second, what's stopping them from getting it? And third, what have they already tried? Now, I I a good example to use is a walking pad. Imagine we're selling a compact walking pad to people who work from home. We start reading reviews and customer feedback and we see a few things like, I sit at my desk for 8 hours and realize I barely moved. Or, I want a treadmill but I don't really have space for one. Maybe another comment that we see is, I'd use one during work but I can't have something super loud while I'm on the calls. And internally I'm thinking, well perfect because this is exactly what we want. Those are our ads. They are the core reason why someone wants this product in the first place and those can be the ideas behind the ads. And so now we have a direction and we can think what format of creative can communicate those core ideas. UGC to tell the story? Can a static image do the job effectively? That thought itself is more important than the format. We have some clients where the product is easy to understand and the value is very straightforward. You don't really need a video to explain it. There's no explanation needed. So a static image can work great and it does for them. But we have other clients where a static won't really paint the whole picture on why the product is valuable. Maybe we have to see something fold open. Maybe we have to see someone get some value in real world utility. These are things that a simple static image cannot show. So that's the core. What format communicates the value? Essentially, we have to pick one problem. Now there's a place where I think brands get themselves into trouble. They are so close to their product and you know, they've been manufacturing it and setting up the store and they try to put all these selling points into one creative. All of the value and the dimensions, the 30-day return, the guarantee, this walking pad is quiet, compact, easy to store, helps you exercise, has the motor, has the speed, you know, the warranty, the 30-day returns. Okay. Well now we've got an infomercial when someone was just watching a cat video the reel before. Instead, pick an argument for the persona that you're targeting. For example, [music] we can say, get more steps while you work without needing a giant treadmill taking precious space. That itself would be one angle. Now, everything [music] inside of that creative should support that idea. Not the 30-day return or the promise, they'll learn all of that later on the landing page. Show a room how there's still lots of space with the walking pad in there, maybe how it's able to slide under a desk, how it can fold or people can easily move it into a closet. And if the product is actually quiet enough to use while working, well, maybe a video of a important call or some sort of interview where someone, you know, has to take it very serious, but then the camera kind of zooms out and now they're getting their steps in. So, the person physically watching that ad thinks that they don't have to compromise health for business or success. You really painted the value without even talking about the treadmill itself. Now, imagine those ads versus a static image of a product with the white background and text saying at home treadmill. It doesn't paint the picture. communicate the real value people get from your product. You're seeing the metal rectangle and not necessarily the core reason why you're buying. Now, don't get me wrong, like that rectangle might work for someone who's already sold, right? Very high intent, they need a treadmill, they've already sold themselves on it. It's just who do I buy from, when is the right time? High intent audiences, but for most cold traffic, they need the picture painted. They need to feel excited about the value and that excitement is what's going to get them to the landing page and ultimately buy. And this is something I really want people to understand. One product can have 10 different reasons why someone might buy it and those 10 reasons can often become 10 different creative angles. When you have the budget to afford it, of course, and not just one giant ad trying to explain all 10. This is where the volume comes in to where if you build one angle up, you get that profitable, now you can have side budget to test the other angles. And next, we want to build the creative around the angle we found. And once I have that, building the actual ad becomes much easier. And let's say our customer problem is, "I work from home all day and barely move." Can sit The hook on our ad can simply be, "If you work from home and somehow finish the day with 800 steps when your goal was 10,000, keep listening." And that's a pretty direct hook, right? The person who resonates with it is going to stop and listen. Then, we introduce the solution. Maybe this walking pad fits underneath your standing desk, lets you get steps in while you work and can be put away when you're finished. And if we have some sort of video ad, the ad can show that whole process. Show someone working at the desk, show the walking pad underneath, show them on a call, show them putting it away afterward. And that itself is the creative. You almost don't even need text overlay or anything like that. And notice something here. We're not trying to be like super clever. We're trying to make the customer understand, and if it resonates with their life, it will really click subconsciously for them and potentially lead them to want to buy. And if we can get them to say, "This solves my exact problem," that's usually a lot more powerful than trying to make the world's most cinematic ad that appeals to everybody. So, when I speak to my clients internally, we always identify why a customer would find value in their product. We look to reviews, we see some topics mentioned pretty consistently, and then we're able to build ads from that, hitting the core reason why the customer would buy it. We sell some blackout blinds in in the reviews in the very beginning, we noticed that people were using them for the nursery, people were using them in RVs, and people were using and truck drivers were using them in their trucks. So, we were able to build creative off of that when initially we just had creative for blackout blinds. But, up until this point, the idea and the pain point generally isn't enough. Your creative also needs proof. And this is a big one because every time you make a claim in an ad, you should be asking, "How can I prove this visually?" If we say it's compact, we want to see how small it actually is. If we say it fits underneath the desk, we have to show it underneath the desk in the ad. And if we say it stores easily, we have to show somebody storing it in an apartment closet or the ability to move it easily, even maybe 55-plus year-olds, etc., etc. And if you're making a product claim that can be quantified and the brand has the data to actually support it, we have to show the actual number. But, the creative should do as much of the selling as possible visually because anybody can say, "Well, this product is amazing. This product changed my life." It's the best product in the northeast and it's the best walking pad ever. Okay, like everybody has heard that and with AI these days, like a lot of people don't even trust it anymore. We have to show why. Now, when we identify all of this, we want to create some variations. We don't want to create just random new ads. And this is where [music] we get into the actual creative testing because let's say I like this angle. Get your steps in while you work without needing a giant treadmill. I don't want to necessarily abandon that idea and make 10 completely different ads. I might make two versions here. Version one, maybe that's a UGC video. Version two could be a carousel where the slides tell the story. General same angle, the same product, same argument, different opening. Now, if one massively outperforms the others, we've actually learned something. And I know video and carousel, you know, there may be a very big difference, but you use this in your own scenarios here. And when you do find something, then we can discuss what's the best kind of ad to make next. And all of this is a big part of how we approach paid media [music] at ADVT. We're not interested in just throwing creative into an account. In a lot of cases, it takes a lot of time and budget to make all of those creatives. We want to understand why something worked with the customer so we can build on it. And if you're an established [music] e-commerce brand and your team is constantly just making ads, but you're still not sure what's actually [music] holding your growth back, you can go to the link in the description or advt-media.net and book a call with us. Now, let's talk about the testing side because this is where most brands can completely ruin good creative. [music] I see this all the time. A brand has a relatively small advertising budget, and they launch 30 new ads, and they're getting ready to launch 20 next week. Then, 2 days later, they say, "This creative doesn't work." And when we look at the account, we say, "Well, based on what?" All that happened was uploaded, and then the spend just kept going to the same one ad. The new stuff never got any budget. So, don't get me wrong. Like, I I've seen marketing teams say, "Well, we tested it, and yeah, the intent was there, but it wasn't really tested." You have to match your creative testing volume to your budget. So, if you're spending 30, 50, $100 a day, you can't feed an unlimited number of ads enough spend to actually learn anything. I'd rather test a focused batch and give Facebook enough opportunity to distribute spend and give me some kind of signal. So, the next stuff we make isn't really blind. It's based on the real customers. And on the other side, I don't really crown something a winner just because it drives the most of your sales. I've gotten on a lot of calls recently where people think they have a winning ad, but when we actually look in the ad account, it's the only thing that got spend. So, of course it's driving sales. It's out in the market more than anything else. It just has the volume behind it. It doesn't mean you actually found the next creative that's going to take your business to $10 million. Now, just last week, we started working with a new account spending $30 a day, and I'm going to show you our exact creative test. In here, you can see that we launched 13 ads. They're spending $30 a day, so we don't have really that much budget here. I initially set our impression limit to 1,000, just so we can get done with this test pretty quickly. But, I noticed that our CPMs were on average like 50, 60, 70 dollars. And so, that means, and I I saw the comments from the other video, you know, $17 CPA is really unrealistic. This is a little bit more realistic with a newer account with a pixel that doesn't have much data to lower our CPM. And so, with that, we had to lower our impression limit to 800 just to make sure that we finish this test efficiently without blowing through a ton of budget. We want to find winners within the first week to two weeks. And so, with this account specifically, I already noticed after a handful of days, there are some learnings here that we can look at. This ad right here, it started spending the most on the very first day. And so, if we just let Facebook run and do their thing, they would have kept spending on this until it spent 150, 200, $400. And the thing is, they're snowballing the volume here because they see the amazing CTR, they see the good link click-through rate, they see the lower than average CPM, and they're going to keep spending here just because they're looking at those supporting metrics and making the decision to say that, "Well, the people on our platform actually like this ad. We're going to keep spending on it." In our service, we don't really take that as face value. We understand why these things are working. Now, let's watch this ad very quickly to see why it might be engaging. And so, if you see here, this is a very visually stimulating ad, right? It's something that catches attention. It's kind of like you want to watch it. It's like those cutting videos or like the you know those videos that are like very um calming to watch essentially. And so, people get engaged with this, but the very core thing is that the customer doesn't really know what we're selling here. They don't know the value of this product here. It's just a very visually stimulating ad. And we can see that with our CTR numbers here. We have a 10.9%. This is actually like a very high CTR for e-commerce, but it almost doesn't matter because look at the supporting metrics here. It led to very little buying behavior weren't primed. They didn't know what they were watching. They didn't even know if they were a customer for this, right? They may not have even wanted a product like this, but the ad caught their attention. It didn't really sell them on the back end. Now, if we look down here to this ad with a 6.3, and it still has a healthy link click-through rate, a pretty medium average kind of CPM, but it actually led to buying behavior on the website because this video actually showed the routine. It showed the before and after. It showed how to apply the product. It showed what you're actually buying. So, the people who watched this ad, maybe overall was a little bit less because lower click-through rate, but look at here. We also look at every other supporting metric because if we look at link click-through rate, this actually is a smaller bridge. Of course, we want to make sure that the people who watched the ad actually click through to the website. Even this ad up here, it has a little bit higher engagement. We have over a 3% drop from CTR to CTR link click-through. And so, what that tells us is we're losing about over 3% of the people because maybe the ad isn't doing that job in explaining the product to explain the value. But this one has less than a 2%. So, that means the people who saw it, more overall people clicked through to the website and were actually primed to buy. And so, although this one engaged higher, you it had a larger drop, percentage drop to the site, and nobody was sold, and nobody understood the value beforehand to want to make a purchase. But this ad here caught less overall attention. The people who actually watched it were sold on the process and the before and after and the result. And so, when they got to the website, now it was basically a vehicle to get them to the purchase. And so, this is really interesting findings. We're going to keep running this creative test and see what else we can find because if we can move forward with this and consistently get a three times or higher return, well, that's going to be ultimately the goal here. And after we identify our winning ads, we want to do one variable at a time. And like I've talked about in other videos, that's going to be the important piece and one of the biggest things that I preach while testing, which is identify your variables. If I change the hook, the angle, the audience here, the landing page, the offer, the campaign, the creative all at the same time, well, what did we test? Nothing, really. Let's say the performance improves. Awesome, but what change actually caused that? We don't really have any idea, right? So, whenever possible, I want to keep enough things stable so that I can actually isolate what I'm learning. So, when you have your two ad ideas like the UGC and the carousel like we talked about before, make sure you test them in an apples-to-apples environment like this creative test and allow them to get equal visibility and then look at the data to identify why something was better. Don't just let one ad get the spend and assume that this is your winner. Because when you do this apples-to-apples test, then you can cut the worst ad and focus on how you can make a better [music] next creative. We can probably do more before and after and actually showing the routine of someone using this product. This is basically the philosophy of this whole CT, LT, everything, these stairway to paid ads heaven. You identify the variable, test it, find a winner, and then move up to the next variable and leaving behind everything weighing you down even if it's a little bit, even if it's 5 cent cost per [music] click. And testing creative should work the exact same way. But make sure you understand the metrics and what they mean so you can really identify why a winner is a winner. And please don't look to just CPA. There's a lot more to the story than just return on ad spend and CPA. And so, when you read why the creative won or lost, you have to think about the customer journey like how we saw here. First, did we get their attention? If nobody stops, maybe the hook isn't strong enough. Maybe the visual itself just isn't that interesting. Then we ask, did they click to the site? If people are watching and nobody's clicking, well, maybe the creative is entertaining but the product and the value isn't compelling or even being communicated. Maybe they don't understand why they need this product. [music] And then you have to ask yourself, well, what happened with my data after the click? If an ad gets a ton of quality clicks but nobody buys, don't [music] blame the creative right away. Maybe you actually have a really good ad because it's the vehicle to the website, driving people to the website, but maybe the landing page is loading slow or it's actually just overall not that good. With that, we're looking at conversion rates, your add to carts, your checkouts, your offer, your pricing, your shipping, your website experience. All of that plays a role. I tell everybody it's a two-piece puzzle. You need your cost to acquire attention and your conversion rate. There's no use in sending a million people to the website if we're only converting at a 0.5. The cost to drive that a million people is never going to be profitable. And so, we have to ask if the ad can actually hold spend at a larger scale as well. And so, all of these metrics, all combined, tell us if the ad can actually hold spend at a larger scale because you can have an ad that looks amazing at $30 a day, but it falls apart the moment you scale it or try to increase budget because you're not really looking at the supporting metrics. You may be only looking at your CPA. A good CPA doesn't necessarily mean a that it's a good ad. Maybe it just works at lower spend or maybe it'd be a great retargeting ad. But these supporting metrics really tell you what should be top of funnel, middle of funnel, and bottom of funnel. And when you can mold and place each ad, handpick them into the places of the funnel, now you can get the result that you want. Let the result tell you what to make next. And this is the part that I feel like most brands really miss because every creative test should be your next creative brief. Because let's say that a certain angle worked, well, great. Let's make more creatives around that angle. Let's say one hook crushed the others, well, great. Let's do that hook, but then like three different bodies of video after that. Or another example is let's say UGC underperformed just like, you know, the review style, but a simple product demonstration actually worked really well. Let's explore more product demonstration creatives. This is how you actually build a creative machine just sitting down every Monday and asking, "Can we get AI to make more static images?" Well, we've been doing this for 2 weeks and aren't really getting results. Instead, we could be saying, "Well, this is what the customers responded to last week. We saw that this concept came up in some of our ads. And so, what if we make UGC talking about this concept, this selling angle?" We also saw how our competitor, some of their reviews are saying that they don't really do that very well. So, if we can combat objection in the ad, maybe this is going to be something that differentiates our product and makes people want to look at it a little bit more outside of just a generic, "Hey, we have this and it's really good." With that, there's a huge difference. So, for your next creative round, choose one customer problem. Write the angle in a single sentence, and make every line of that ad >> [music] >> prove that sentence. Then, change one meaningful thing at a time, and let the result tell you what to build next. And [music] if you're looking to see what the results are actually telling you, watch If You Don't Understand Data, You Don't Understand Facebook Ads Next. It shows you what numbers matter before you scale, cut, or rebuild a creative.
